Section 2: Four-Cycle Engine Theory Introduction Four events must occur in the correct sequence and at the correct time for the engine to run correctly. These events are (A) intake, (B) compression, (C) ignition and power, and (D) exhaust. (A) Intake (C) Power Four-Cycle Engine Theory 001684 The piston is traveling from top dead center (TDC) to bottom dead center (BDC). The cam has opened the intake valve. The piston's downward movement in the cylinder creates a partial vacuum in the cylinder. Air at atmospheric pressure is drawn into the cylinder through the carburetor and is mixed with fuel in the carburetor. The fuel-air mixture flows through the open intake valve into the cylinder. The intake stroke is complete when the piston reaches BDC. (B) Compression 001686 Combustion is already in progress when the piston reaches TDC. The intake and exhaust valves remain closed as expanding gases of combustion force the piston downward. (D) Exhaust 001687 The exhaust stroke begins when the piston has reached BDC and has started its upward movement. The intake valve is closed, and the exhaust valve is open to let gases escape. 001685 As the piston reaches BDC, both the intake and exhaust valves are closed. The piston moves upward toward TDC and the fuel-air mixture is compressed. Ignition occurs just before the piston reaches TDC. G-Force V-Twin Engine Service Manual 9

Systematic Inspection If engine will not start and the cause of malfunction is not readily apparent, perform a systematic inspection in the following order: 1. Fuel 2. Ignition 3. Compression This inspection, performed in a systematic manner, can usually be done in a matter of minutes. It is the quickest and surest method of determining the cause of failure. The basic inspection procedure is the same for all engine models. Any variation, by model, will be described under the subject heading. Checking Fuel Fuel pressure on LP and NG generator engines can be checked using a pressure test kit for LP and NG systems. For gasoline engines, check the following: • Is the fuel tank full? • Is the fuel stale? • Is the tank vent open? • Is the fuel shutoff valve open? • Is the fuel pump working? • Is the fuel solenoid working? Checking Ignition See Ignition for testing procedures. Checking Compression Proceed as follows to check engine compression: 1. Remove both spark plugs and insert a compression gauge (Generac P/N GN04001) into either cylinder (one cylinder at a time). 2. Open throttle to wide open throttle (WOT) position. 3. Turn engine over with engine starter until there is no further increase in pressure. Record this reading. 4. Repeat procedure on other cylinder and record reading. The compression difference between both cylinders should not exceed 25%. More than 25% indicates loss of compression in the cylinder with lower pressure. General Information To calculate the difference in percentage, divide the difference in PSI (kPa) by the higher pressure reading. See examples below. Engine #1 Engine #2 Engine #3 Cylinder 1 165 psi (1137.6 kPa) 175 psi (1206.6 kPa) 160 psi (1103.1 kPa) Cylinder 2 160 psi (1103.1 kPa) 155 psi (1068.7 kPa) 112 psi (772.2 kPa) Difference 5 psi (34.5 kPa) 20 psi (137.9 kPa) 48 psi (330.9 kPa) Engine #1: (5 psi ÷ 165 psi) [34.5 kPa ÷ 1103.1 kPa] = 0.03 = 3% difference Engine #2: (20 psi ÷ 175 psi) [137.9 kPa ÷ 1206.6 kPa} = 0.11 = 11% difference Engine #3: (48 psi ÷ 160 psi) [330.9 kPa ÷ 1103.1 kPa] = 0.30 = 30% difference Using this method of calculation, Cylinder 2 in Engine #3 has lost significant compression. If compression is poor, look for one or more of the following causes: • Loose cylinder head bolts • Failed cylinder head gasket • Burned / worn valves or valve seats • Insufficient valve clearance • Warped cylinder head • Warped valve stem or worn valve guides • Worn or broken piston ring(s) • Worn or damaged cylinder bore • Broken connecting rod Model GH816 EPT/HSB Normal Compression 180–220 psi (1240–1520 kPa) G-Force V-Twin Engine Service Manual 13

Section 7: Electric Starter Electric Starter General Information See Figure 7-1. The starter motor utilizes a solenoid, similar to an automobile starter, to assist in pinion gear engagement. When the starter motor is activated, the pinion gear engages a ring gear attached to the engine flywheel and cranks the engine. Figure 7-1. Starter Motor sw0095 Troubleshooting IMPORTANT NOTE: Do not rotate engine with electric starter while spark plugs are removed, unless using a compression gauge. Arcing at the spark plug ends may ignite gasoline vapor exiting the spark plug hole. NOTE: If a starting problem is encountered, inspect the engine thoroughly to eliminate it as the cause of starting difficulty. Check engine for free rotation by removing spark plugs and flywheel guard and turning the crankshaft with a socket and ratchet or breaker bar. Verify it rotates freely. Engine cranks slowly: • Additional drag on engine, affecting starter performance (see note above). • Discharged battery. • Faulty electrical connection (battery circuit). • Dirty or worn starter motor commutator, bearing, weak magnets, worn brushes, etc. • Incorrect oil viscosity for temperature expected. • Battery leads too long or wire too small. • Underpowered battery. Engine will not crank if: • Faulty safety interlocks. • Discharged battery. • Faulty electrical connections. • Faulty starter motor switch (open circuit). • Open circuit in starter motor. • Brushes sticking, etc. • Faulty solenoid. Section 8: Lubrication System Lubrication System Description Generac GH-816 G-Force V-twins use a full pressure lubrication system with an oil filter. A gerotor oil pump draws oil from a screened oil pickup in the sump and pumps oil through the oil filter. Filtered oil flows through an oil gallery in the sump and is distributed to the main bearings, connecting rod bearings, hydraulic lash adjusters, and camshaft bearings. Engine oil pressure varies with oil viscosity, ambient air temperature differences, operating temperatures, and engine load. Oil Pressure - @ 70 °F (21 °C): 15–50 psi (103–345 kPa) NOTE: A pressure relief valve limits the maximum oil pressure in the system to 30–40 psi (206–276 kPa). Protection Systems Low Oil Pressure Switch See Figure 8-1. The engine is usually equipped with a normally open type, low oil pressure switch (A) which closes the circuit between the terminals when oil pressure drops below 10 psi (69 kPa). The engine will shut down on low oil pressure if one terminal is connected to the ignition ground wire and the other terminal is connected to ground. The low oil pressure switch can also be connected to an alarm or light to indicate low oil pressure, instead of shutting down the engine. A 009616 Figure 8-1. Low Oil Pressure Switch A delay built into the shutdown system on some engine applications allows oil pressure to build during starting. The delay allows the engine to run for about 10 seconds before sensing oil pressure. The engine shuts down if the engine is wired for low oil pressure shutdown and the system senses low oil pressure during operation. The engine will not run until 8 psi (55 kPa) of oil pressure is reached. If a restart is attempted within five seconds after shutdown, the engine may NOT start. The system needs 10 seconds to reset. Checking Engine Oil Level Oil capacity of the GH/GTV-816 G-Force engine is approximately 2 qt (1.9L). See Specifications for the recommended amount for each model. Proceed as follows to check the engine oil level: 1. See Figure 8-2. Remove oil dipstick (A) and wipe it dry with a clean cloth. A 009616 Figure 8-2. Oil Fill/Dipstick Location 2. Insert oil dipstick completely, then remove. Oil level should be at the FULL mark. If necessary, add oil until the FULL mark is reached. Do not fill above the FULL mark. CAUTION Engine damage. Verify proper type and quantity of engine oil prior to starting engine. Failure to do so could result in engine damage. Cylinder Finish (Cross Hatch) Recondition cylinder bores to restore cross hatch before installing new piston rings in a cylinder within specification. Avoid honing cylinder bores oversize. Oversize cylinder bores will permanently damage the crankcase. See Figure 9-4. Special honing stones are required when reconditioning a cylinder bore. Honing stones produce the correct cross hatch necessary for correct lubrication and ring seating. Honing is performed as a two step process called plateau honing. These steps must be followed carefully, and should be performed by a competent machine shop. The correct cross hatch angle is approximately 45º. 45º Figure 9-4. Cylinder Cross Hatch 004359 Honing is done with a variable speed 1/2 in portable drill and a honing fixture. Figure 9-6 at the end of this topic provides dimensions for making a honing fixture. Setup 1. See Figure 9-5. Use two crankcase cover mounting screws to fasten honing fixture (A) to crankcase. A Figure 9-5. Honing Cylinders 004360 2. Cut a wood block and place inside crankcase to prevent hone from extending further than 0.75–1.0 in (19 mm–25 mm) below cylinder bore. 3. Clamp honing fixture and crankcase securely in a vise at a convenient work height. Cylinder and Crankcase Cover 4. Place hone in middle of cylinder bore. Tighten adjusting knob with fingers until stones fit snugly against cylinder wall. DO NOT FORCE. Place hone drive shaft in portable drill chuck and tighten. Verify cylinder and hone are centered and aligned with drill spindle. Honing Procedure Proceed as follows to hone the cylinder: 1. For the first pass, hone each cylinder with a 220 grit diamond metal-bond super-abrasive stone (such as a Sunnen® GMG55). Set drill speed at 240 rpm at 80 strokes per minute. Lubricate cylinder liberally to prevent buildup on honing stones. 2. For the second pass, hone each cylinder with an 800 grit diamond metal-bond super-abrasive stone (such as a Sunnen® RMG807) at 110 rpm drill speed at 80 strokes per minute. NOTE: Sunnen® lubricating oil (SCC605) is recommended. Automatic transmission fluid is also an acceptable honing oil. Another acceptable honing oil can be made by mixing four parts 30 weight oil with one part kerosene. Cleaning Proceed as follows to clean each cylinder and crankcase thoroughly after honing: 1. Wash cylinder and crankcase carefully in a commercial solvent or kerosene. 2. Thoroughly wash cylinder and crankcase using a stiff brush with soap and hot water. Rinse thoroughly with hot running water. 3. Repeat washing and rinsing until all traces of honing grit are gone. IMPORTANT NOTE: Honing grit is highly abrasive and will cause rapid wear to all internal components of the engine unless it is completely removed. 4. Use a clean white rag or paper towel and wipe the cylinder bore when cylinder and crankcase have been thoroughly cleaned. Any remaining honing grit will be visible as a gray residue. Wash and rinse entire cylinder and crankcase if any honing grip is evident, and inspect again. The cylinder has been correctly cleaned when there is no trace of honing grit on the rag. Apply oil to the cylinder bore to prevent rusting. G-Force V-Twin Engine Service Manual 47

Section 12: Troubleshooting Troubleshooting Problem Solving Introduction Problems affecting engine operation may be classified as one of, or a combination of two or more of the following: • Engine will not start. • Engine starts with difficulty. • Engine lacks power. • Engine vibrates. • Engine overheats. • Engine burns oil. In many cases, the cause will be readily apparent. If this is not the case, inspect the fuel system, ignition system, and engine compression. These inspections can be performed quickly and are the best methods of finding the cause of a failure. They may also provide early detection of future failures. Checking Fuel System For gasoline powered engines, verify fuel tank has been correctly filled with correct fuel. If engine is equipped with a fuel shutoff valve, verify valve is open. Verify fuel is flowing through fuel line and to carburetor. Adjust carburetor as needed. Verify choke closes completely. If engine does not start, remove and inspect spark plug. If spark plug is WET, look for the following: • Overchoking. • Dirty air cleaner. • Excessively rich fuel-air mixture. • Water in fuel. • Fuel leaking past carburetor float needle. If spark plug is DRY, look for the following: • Carburetor mounting gasket leaks. • Dirt or gum in carburetor or fuel line. • Carburetor float needle stuck closed. • Inoperative fuel pump (if equipped). • Clogged fuel filter (if equipped). Checking Ignition System See Ignition. Checking Compression Proceed as follows to check engine compression: 1. Remove spark plug. 2. Insert an automotive type compression gauge into the spark plug hole. 3. Crank engine until there is no further increase in pressure. The highest reading obtained is engine compression pressure. If compression is poor, inspect for one or more of the following causes: • Loose cylinder head bolts. • Failed cylinder head gasket. • Burned valves or valve seats. • Insufficient valve clearance. • Warped cylinder head. • Warped valve stem. • Worn or broken piston ring(s). • Worn or damaged cylinder bore. • Broken connecting rod. • Worn valve seats or valves. • Worn valve guides.
